newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland official faces renewed Catholic ire.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland official faces renewed Catholic ire.

text.p: Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, faced increasing Catholic anger on Tuesday over a leaked official document which suggested she had ignored their objections to a weekend Protestant parade.

Mowlam went into a new round of Northern Ireland peace talks overshadowed by Catholic ire over the document, which concluded that allowing the parade along Portadown's Catholic Garvaghy Road was "the least worst outcome".
But it resulted in the worst unrest seen in Northern Ireland for years, overshadowing the latest session of the year-old multi-party talks between pro-British Unionists and pro-Irish nationalists.

Participants say the negotiations are marking time, dogged by the alarming security situation in which two police have been shot and wounded, one hundred people hurt and the province gripped by nightly Catholic rioting and shooting.
Pro-British Loyalist groups emerged from the shadows of the conflict to stage an ominous show of force in which they said they would "defend" Protestant areas from Catholic attack.

Mowlam said that Catholic residents groups opposed to Protestant weekend marches were not speaking to her after the authorities allowed an Orange Order parade last Sunday over the objections of Catholic residents who felt it was intimidation.

She said she would continue to seek an agreement to avert further violence when the Orange Order marches along Belfast's Lower Ormeau Road on Saturday at the climax of the annual marching season by pro-British Protestant organisations.
"Nationalists are very angry. Nationalists are thinking about whether to talk to me or not so my use may be limited after my failure in Garvaghy. I accept that," she said.

Mowlam disputed media reports based on a leaked Northern Ireland Office (NIO) document which purported to show that her advisers decided to permit the Orange Order march back on June 20, 15 days before a decision was announced and greeted by riots.
The embattled British official did not dispute the authenticity of the NIO document but said it was merely a summary of options drawn up by security advisers.
Catholic anger continued to burn. A policeman patrolling disturbances on Portadown's Garvaghy Road was shot and wounded as Catholics kept up a barrage of protest across the province.

Suspected Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas, fighting British rule of the province, or a sister group were believed responsible for his injuries and for a series of armed attacks on British troops and police during overnight Catholic riots.

Since Saturday night there have been 776 attacks on the security forces, 1,444 petrol bombings and 363 hijackings. A total of 60 police and 49 civilians have been injured and police and troops have fired 2,400 plastic bullets to quell riots.
Police said rioting erupted overnight in Catholic parts of Belfast and in the towns of Newry, Portadown, Lurgan and Strabane, where police fired 200 plastic bullets to keep order.
Although on a lower scale than on previous nights, the violence showed no sign of abating in the run-up to parades on Saturday in Belfast and Londonderry. the province's second city.
To date Loyalists have taken no part in the violence. But Ulster Television showed footage of a show of force by six armed men who said their organisation would defend Protestant areas.
Some Protestants whose houses adjoin Catholic areas of Belfast said that their homes had been targeted by Catholic youths in a nightly assault with petrol bombs and rocks.
Loyalists are officially observing a truce with the IRA they called in October 1994, but have been blamed by police for a series of attacks against Catholic targets in the past six months.
Police were investigating the death of a Protestant youth who apparently died in an explosion in south Belfast but refused to confirm or deny speculation that he was handling a bomb.
Mowlam, said the circumstances surrounding his death were unclear but added: "One death is one death too many. Northern Ireland has seen too much tragedy. Violence solves nothing."

It was the sole fatality reported since the violence exploded on Saturday immediately after the Orange Order marched down the Garvaghy Road to celebrate what it called a birthright with a peaceful demonstration on a stretch of public highway.
